10 Tools Every Classic-Car Owner Should Have
Updated: Oct 17

The best classic-car tool collection is not the biggest one. It is the collection that helps you diagnose before replacing, protects irreplaceable parts and lets you work deliberately instead of improvising. These are ten tools we consider foundational for anyone who owns, maintains or restores an older car.
Every item below can be found in The Fitzgerald Classics Garage, where we keep the tools and products we actually recommend for restoration and preservation work.
1. Quality Digital Multimeter

Quality Digital Multimeter — Electrical problems are part of classic-car ownership. A dependable multimeter lets you verify voltage, continuity, resistance, grounds, charging-system performance and whether a component is actually receiving power before you start replacing parts.
2. Click-Type or Electronic Torque Wrench

Click-Type or Electronic Torque Wrench — Classic cars reward careful assembly. A good torque wrench helps you tighten critical fasteners correctly instead of relying on feel, whether you are working on wheels, suspension, engine accessories or other components with specified torque values.
3. Complete 3/8-Inch Drive Socket Set

Complete 3/8-Inch Drive Socket Set — This is one of the most-used tool sets in our garage. A broad mix of shallow and deep sockets gives you the flexibility to handle routine maintenance, teardown and reassembly without constantly stopping to hunt for a missing size.
4. Rechargeable LED Work Light

Rechargeable LED Work Light — Good lighting changes everything. A magnetic rechargeable light makes under-dash work, engine-bay troubleshooting and work underneath the car easier while leaving both hands free.
5. Non-Marring Trim Removal Tool Kit

Non-Marring Trim Removal Tool Kit — Old trim, bezels and interior panels are increasingly hard to replace. Plastic trim tools give you leverage without immediately reaching for a screwdriver that can scar paint, vinyl or brightwork.
6. Smart Battery Charger and Maintainer

Smart Battery Charger and Maintainer — Many classics sit more than they drive. A quality smart maintainer helps keep the battery ready without the crude constant charging associated with older chargers.
7. LED Inspection Flashlight

LED Inspection Flashlight — A compact, powerful inspection light is invaluable when evaluating a car or chasing a problem. Use it to inspect frame areas, wiring, casting numbers, leaks, corrosion, body seams and spaces that overhead garage lighting simply cannot reach.
8. Telescoping Inspection Mirror

Telescoping Inspection Mirror — Sometimes the thing you need to see is exactly where your head cannot go. An inspection mirror is inexpensive, takes almost no room in the toolbox and routinely saves time when looking behind engines, dashboards and brackets.
9. Digital Caliper

Digital Caliper — Restoration work involves far more measurement than many people expect. A digital caliper is useful for checking hardware, shafts, bushings, trim dimensions, gaps and unknown parts before ordering replacements.
10. Magnetic Parts Trays

Magnetic Parts Trays — A restoration can be lost one tiny fastener at a time. Magnetic trays keep nuts, bolts, clips and washers together during disassembly and dramatically reduce the chance of original hardware disappearing.
What We Would Buy First

If you are starting from scratch, begin with the multimeter, socket set, torque wrench and LED work light. Those four tools cover an enormous amount of routine maintenance and troubleshooting. From there, add the inspection tools and specialty items as your projects demand them.
Build the Garage Around the Work

Tools should earn their place. We would rather own one reliable tool that gets used for years than three cheaper versions that create frustration or uncertainty. That same philosophy guides the Fitzgerald Classics Garage: useful products, real restoration applications and recommendations tied to the work rather than a catalog full of things nobody needs.
